##Feature selection
```{r}
#Best subset selection in logistic regression
#Best subset wasnt applied since it has  limitation of p<=15, however our dataset has 18 variables. Although it is a good method, it has a high computational time.
library(bestglm)

best.logit <- bestglm(crashes, IC = "AIC", family = binomial, method = "exhaustive")
summary(best.logit$BestModel)
best.logit$Subsets
```

```{r}
#Forward stepwise selection in logistic regression
full.model = glm(severity ~ ., family=binomial, data=crashes)
null.model = glm(severity ~ 1, family=binomial, data=crashes)

summary(stepAIC(null.model, # start with a model containing no variables
                direction = 'forward', # run forward selection
                scope = list(upper = full.model, # the maximum to consider is a model with all variables
                             lower = null.model), # the minimum to consider is a model with no variables
                trace = 0))
```

```{r}
#Backward stepwise selection in logistic regression
full.model = glm(severity ~ ., family=binomial, data=crashes)
null.model = glm(severity ~ 1, family=binomial, data=crashes)

summary(stepAIC(full.model, # start with a model containing no variables
                direction = 'backward', # run backward selection
                scope = list(upper = full.model, # the maximum to consider is a model with all variables
                             lower = null.model), # the minimum to consider is a model with no variables
                trace = 0))
```



```{r}
#lasso in logistic regression
set.seed (10)
cv.lasso <- cv.glmnet(x, y, alpha=1, nfolds=10, family ="binomial")
plot(cv.lasso)
bestlam.2 <- cv.lasso$lambda.min

#Fit the lasso model on training dataset
lasso_train <- glmnet(x_train,y_train,family = "binomial", alpha = 1, lambda = bestlam.2)
lasso_train$beta

#Make predictions on test data
lasso.pred <- predict(lasso_train, s =bestlam.2,newx = x_test)
lasso.pred.classes <- ifelse(lasso.pred>0.5, "1", "0")

mean(lasso.pred.classes==y_test)
table(lasso.pred.classes, y_test)

#confusion matrix
confusionMatrix(as.factor(lasso.pred.classes),y_test, mode="everything", positive = "1")
ROC_lasso <- roc(y_test,as.numeric(lasso.pred.classes))

auc(ROC_lasso) #Area under the curve is0.531

plot(roc.glmnet(lasso_train, newx = x_test, newy=y_test))
```
##Logistic Regression
```{r}
# Assuming 'your_data' is your data frame
Logit_model = glm(severity ~ dayofwk+lightcond+alcohol+drug+traffic_signal+relationtord+ nolanes+truckinv+intersection+direction+     gender+age+speedlmt, data = rose_data, family=binomial)

summary(Logit_model)

#testing the accuracy of the data
predict_logit = predict(Logit_model, newdata=test_data)
summary(predict_logit)

predictlogit.classes <- ifelse(predict_logit > 0.5, 1,0)

confusionMatrix(as.factor(predictlogit.classes),y_test, mode="everything", positive = "1")
ROC_logit <- roc(y_test,as.numeric(predictlogit.classes))

roc_logit <- roc(y_test, predictlogit.classes)
auc(ROC_logit) 
plot(roc_logit, main = "ROC Curve for Logistic Regression", col = "red", lwd = 1.5)
# Add AUC to the plot
text(0.8, 0.2, paste("AUC =", round(auc(ROC_logit), 3)), col = "blue", cex = 1.1)
```



#Fitting a random forest
```{r}
#Cross validation to find the number of variables randomly sampled
# Install and load necessary packages
# install.packages("caret")
library(caret)

# Assuming your_data is your dataset and response is your binary target variable

# Set up a control object for 5-fold cross-validation
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5)

# Create a vector of candidate mtry values
candidate_mtry <- c(1, round(sqrt(ncol(rose_data) - 1)), ncol(rose_data) - 1)

# Fit models with different mtry values using cross-validation
model_results <- list()

for (m in candidate_mtry) {
  rf_model <- train(severity ~dayofwk+lightcond+alcohol+drug+traffic_signal+relationtord+ nolanes+truckinv+intersection+direction+     gender+age+speedlmt, data = rose_data, method = "rf",
                    trControl = ctrl, tuneGrid = data.frame(mtry = m),
                    ntree = 500)
  
  model_results[[as.character(m)]] <- rf_model
}

# Print and compare results
for (m in candidate_mtry) {
  cat("mtry =", m, "\n")
  print(model_results[[as.character(m)]])
  cat("\n")
}

# Extract the best mtry based on cross-validated performance
best_mtry <- as.numeric(model_results[[as.character(candidate_mtry[which.min(sapply(model_results, function(model) model$results$Accuracy))])]]$bestTune$mtry)


cat("Best mtry based on cross-validated performance:", best_mtry, "\n")

# Fit the final model with the selected mtry
final_rf_model <- randomForest(severity ~ ., data = rose_data, ntree = 500, mtry = best_mtry)
print(final_rf_model)

varImpPlot(final_rf_model) #Higher values of Mean Decrease Gini indicate higher variable importance.
```

#Testing the accuracy
```{r}
# Make predictions on the training data
pred_rf <- predict(final_rf_model, newdata= test_data, type = "response")

# Create a ROC curve
roc_rfmodel <- roc(test_data$severity, as.numeric(pred_rf))

# Plot the ROC curve
plot(roc_rfmodel, main = "ROC Curve for Random Forest", col = "darkblue", lwd = 2)

# Add AUC to the plot
text(0.8, 0.2, paste("AUC =", round(auc(roc_rfmodel), 3)), col = "green", cex = 1.2)

# Add 45-degree reference line for comparison
abline(a = 0, b = 1, col = "gray", lty = 2)
```
#XGBOOST

```{r}
library(xgboost)
library(pdp)
library(margins)
library(ggplot2)


# Split the data into training and testing sets
set.seed(25)
spl = sample.split(crashes$severity, SplitRatio = 0.80)
train_data = subset(crashes, spl==TRUE)
test_data = subset(crashes, spl==FALSE)

# Remove rows with missing values in the target variable
train_data <- na.omit(train_data, cols = "severity")


# Convert factor predictor variables to numeric

train_data$dayofwk <- as.numeric(as.factor(train_data$dayofwk))
train_data$lightcond<- as.numeric(as.factor(train_data$lightcond))
train_data$alcohol<- as.numeric(as.factor(train_data$alcohol))
train_data$drug<- as.numeric(as.factor(train_data$drug))
train_data$traffic_signal<- as.numeric(as.factor(train_data$traffic_signal))
train_data$relationtord<- as.numeric(as.factor(train_data$relationtord))
train_data$roadcond<- as.numeric(as.factor(train_data$roadcond))
train_data$nolanes<- as.numeric(as.factor(train_data$nolanes))
train_data$truckinv<- as.numeric(as.factor(train_data$truckinv))
train_data$speedlmt<- as.numeric(as.factor(train_data$speedlmt))
train_data$intersection<- as.numeric(as.factor(train_data$intersection))
train_data$direction<- as.numeric(as.factor(train_data$direction))
train_data$gender<- as.numeric(as.factor(train_data$gender))
train_data$age<- as.numeric(as.factor(train_data$age))

# Extract target variable and predictor variables
train_labels <- train_data$severity
train_features <- train_data[, c("dayofwk","lightcond","alcohol","drug", "traffic_signal","relationtord","nolanes", "truckinv","speedlmt" ,"intersection","direction","age", "gender" )]

# Train XGBoost model
xgb_model <- xgboost(data = as.matrix(train_features), label = as.numeric(as.character(train_labels)), objective = "binary:logistic", nrounds = 100)

# Predict on the test set

test_data$dayofwk <- as.numeric(as.factor(test_data$dayofwk))
test_data$lightcond<- as.numeric(as.factor(test_data$lightcond))
test_data$alcohol<- as.numeric(as.factor(test_data$alcohol))
test_data$drug<- as.numeric(as.factor(test_data$drug))
test_data$traffic_signal<- as.numeric(as.factor(test_data$traffic_signal))
test_data$relationtord<- as.numeric(as.factor(test_data$relationtord))
test_data$roadcond<- as.numeric(as.factor(test_data$roadcond))
test_data$nolanes<- as.numeric(as.factor(test_data$nolanes))
test_data$truckinv<- as.numeric(as.factor(test_data$truckinv))
test_data$speedlmt<- as.numeric(as.factor(test_data$speedlmt))
test_data$intersection<- as.numeric(as.factor(test_data$intersection))
test_data$direction<- as.numeric(as.factor(test_data$direction))
test_data$gender<- as.numeric(as.factor(test_data$gender))
test_data$age<- as.numeric(as.factor(test_data$age))

test_labels <- test_data$severity
test_labels <- as.numeric(as.character(test_labels))

test_features <- test_data[,  c("dayofwk","lightcond","alcohol","drug", "traffic_signal","relationtord","nolanes", "truckinv","speedlmt" ,"intersection","direction","age", "gender")]


xgb_pred <- predict(xgb_model, as.matrix(test_features), type = "response", thresholds = common_thresholds, specificity = TRUE)


# Calculate the ROC curve
roc_xgb <- pROC::roc(test_labels, xgb_pred)

# Plot the ROC curve
library(pROC)

# Assuming 'roc_curve' is a roc object
plot.roc(roc_xgb, col = "blue", main = "ROC Curve for XGBoost", col.main = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
text(0.8, 0.2, paste("AUC =", round(auc(roc_curve), 3)), col = "green", cex = 1.0)

```

```{r}
), col = c("blue", "red", "green"), lwd = 2)

```


#Understanding the variables
```{r}
# Install and load the iml package
#install.packages("iml")
# Assuming `xgb_model` is your trained XGBoost model
importance_matrix <- xgb.importance(model = xgb_model)

# Print the importance matrix
print(importance_matrix)

###
#In XGBoost, the feature importance is given by three metrics: Gain, Cover, and Frequency. Here's how you can interpret each of them:
#1. **Gain**: This is the average contribution of the feature to the model across all trees. The higher the value, the more important the feature in contributing to the model. In other words, it implies the total gain of each feature when it is used in trees.

#2. **Cover**: This metric means the relative number of observations related to this feature. It is the number of times a feature is used to split the data across all trees.

#3. **Frequency**: This is the percentage representing the relative number of times a particular feature occurs in the trees of the model.

#In summary, Gain is based on the improvement in accuracy brought by a feature to the branches it is on. Cover measures the number of observations affected by a feature. Frequency is the percentage of trees that use a feature for splitting. All these measures allow you to understand the significance of the features in your model.

```
